mentions.excerpt: Kakashii read the same quarter and found 0.4 gigawatts of compute actually deployed.
Kakashii’s accounting question cuts the other way.

Kakashii’s figures are spectacular: CoreWeave revenue rose from $229 million in 2023 to $5.1 billion in 2025, active power from about 70 megawatts to more than 1.5 gigawatts, and backlog to $104.2 billion.

Kakashii estimates that Nvidia’s plan to ship more than 10 million Blackwell and Rubin chips by the end of 2026 implies roughly 20 gigawatts of power, and holds that Blackwell GPUs ended up in warehouses because too few data centers had cooling and equipment.

Kakashii, on September 24, reads Oracle's first fiscal quarter the other way: most of the $26 billion rise in remaining performance obligations came prepaid or with the customer's own hardware, so the new contracts need no incremental capital from Oracle.

And Kakashii's September 24 point about Oracle is the strongest word on this side: most of the new obligations arrived prepaid or with the customer's own hardware, so they depend on no one raising capital.

Oracle reports on December 9, the day of the Fed's last decision of the year: whether new remaining performance obligations keep arriving prepaid or with the customer's own hardware, the condition for Kakashii's reading that capital spending peaks in fiscal 2027 and 2028.
